summary:
Castilla-La Mancha stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado, applies uniformly across all autonomous communities, including this one, and the source inventory identifies no facility, expression or assembly restriction enacted at regional level.

Document-relevant provision is national and administrative. Adults may request rectification of the sex entry on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, without prior surgical reassignment, a gender-dysphoria diagnosis or two years of medical treatment; the right is grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Constitution. Because access to sex-separated facilities rests on the gender marker recorded in the civil registry rather than on biological sex, that registry entry is the operative basis for facility rules encountered in the region.

Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that proved contentious in the law's passage, and Ley 4/2023 also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Penal protection is national. Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and Article 510 hate speech carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Courts are applying the aggravation in practice: a Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo used the transfobia aggravation for the first time in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman and fined the author EUR 300, and in Valencia a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, with two minors judged separately.

Discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics are defined and sanctioned, discriminatory contract clauses are null and void, and the law combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing while strengthening protections for unmarried same-sex couples.

Violence risk is documented at national level rather than for this region specifically: a 2026 federation report found that 44% of LGBTI respondents had experienced a hate-motivated incident. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.
tangentialFactors:
With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay in the small group of countries offering gender recognition without a medical gatekeeping route. That comparative position shapes what a visitor can expect of the paperwork here: a registry application rather than a clinical process.

The 44% victimisation figure from the 2026 federation report is a national baseline. It indicates the level of reported hate-motivated incident exposure LGBTI people face in Spain as a whole, but it is not broken down for Castilla-La Mancha, so it should be read as context for regional risk rather than a measurement of it.

The contention over the Article-level provision allowing recognition from age 12 shows that parts of the national framework remain politically contested, even while the law is in force and being applied. Enforcement of the aggravating circumstance is nonetheless established, with courts in Vigo and Valencia passing and applying sentences.

Spain's standing in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries sits alongside a documented incidence of hate-motivated incidents, so a favourable ranking should not be read as an absence of street-level or online hostility.
localsOnly:
Residents of Castilla-La Mancha rectify the sex entry on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry under the national procedure, with no diagnosis, surgical requirement or treatment period preceding the request; the right rests on the free development of personality recognised in Article 10.1 of the Constitution.

Ley 4/2023 obliges the collection of discrimination data broken down by the covered causes — sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics — and mandates anti-discrimination measures adapted to rural circumstances, a provision of direct bearing in a region with substantial rural population. It also declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void.

The law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition of gender is possible from age 12 under conditions. Unmarried same-sex couples receive strengthened protections under the same statute, and same-sex marriage with full adoption rights has been in force nationally since 2005.

Residents reporting transphobic conduct can invoke the Article 22.4 aggravating circumstance in sentencing and the Article 510 hate-speech offence, both established under Organic Law 6/2022; there is no separate offence keyed to gender expression.
outOfScopeNotes:
No regional implementing decree, instruction or facility rule specific to the Castilla-La Mancha government appears in the source inventory, and the absence of such material is recorded here as unresolved rather than confirmed. The claim that no sub-national facility, expression or assembly restriction exists anywhere in Spain derives from the national dossier and is not independently sourced for this region.

The inventory supplies no hate-crime counts, victimisation figures or prosecution totals for Castilla-La Mancha. The 44% incidence in the 2026 federation report is a national aggregate with no regional breakdown available here.

Whether a Castilla-La Mancha court has applied the transfobia aggravation is not sourced. The two documented applications cited, in Vigo and Valencia, are national illustrations of judicial practice, not evidence from this region.

Regional-level guidance on how the Civil Registry in this autonomous community handles requests from minors aged 12 to 16, and on the operation of the rural-measures obligation in this territory, remains unsourced.
